reference.source: Kelley & Firestein's Textbook of Rheumatology / IgG4-related disease guidance
clinicalPearls: Part of the IgG4-related disease spectrum, characterised by inflammatory thickening of the aortic wall and surrounding tissue
Periaortitis may extend to encase the ureters and produce retroperitoneal fibrosis with obstructive uropathy
Histology shows a dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate rich in IgG4-positive plasma cells, storiform fibrosis, and obliterative phlebitis
Serum IgG4 is often but not invariably elevated, so a normal level does not exclude the diagnosis
Other organ involvement (pancreas, salivary glands, lacrimal glands) supports the systemic diagnosis
It responds well to glucocorticoids, frequently with steroid-sparing immunosuppression to maintain remission
Aneurysm and dissection risk means structural surveillance accompanies immunosuppression
reference.pathophysiology: IgG4-related aortitis and periaortitis result from the fibroinflammatory process of IgG4-related disease affecting the aorta and periaortic tissues. Aberrant T-follicular helper and B-cell responses drive infiltration by IgG4-positive plasma cells and lymphocytes, with characteristic storiform fibrosis and obliterative phlebitis. Inflammation and fibrosis thicken and weaken the aortic wall while the surrounding fibrotic mass may entrap adjacent structures such as the ureters. Wall damage predisposes to aneurysm formation and dissection.
additionalInvestigations: CT or MR angiography of the aorta and retroperitoneum
Serum IgG4 and IgG subclass measurement
Tissue biopsy showing IgG4-positive plasma cells with storiform fibrosis
PET imaging to map disease extent and other organ involvement
Renal function and urinary tract imaging for obstructive uropathy
Inflammatory markers and assessment for other IgG4-related organ disease
redFlags: Acute chest or back pain suggesting dissection or rupture
Obstructive uropathy with rising creatinine from periureteric fibrosis
reference.prognosis: IgG4-related aortitis usually responds well to immunosuppression with regression of inflammation, but relapse is common and established fibrosis or aneurysm may persist. Prognosis is favourable with treatment and monitoring, though structural complications can require surgical repair.
pitfalls: Excluding the diagnosis because serum IgG4 is normal
Overlooking retroperitoneal extension and obstructive uropathy
Failing to look for other organ manifestations of IgG4-related disease
Relying on immunosuppression alone when an aneurysm needs structural repair
references: International consensus guidance on IgG4-related disease
management: Induce remission with glucocorticoids, which typically produce rapid regression of the aortic wall inflammation
Add a steroid-sparing immunosuppressant or rituximab to maintain remission and manage the common relapses
Monitor with serial CT or MR angiography for aneurysm formation and dissection, alongside serum IgG4 and inflammatory markers
Refer for surgical or endovascular repair of aneurysm or dissection when structural aortic damage is established
Relieve any associated ureteric entrapment and obstructive uropathy with stenting while treating the underlying disease
Screen for and monitor IgG4-related involvement of other organs such as the pancreas and salivary glands
Coordinate care across rheumatology, vascular medicine and surgery
